extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, fiction writers, and students of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how novelists should conceive, present, and balance characters within fiction — covering realism vs art, types of characters (flat/round), treatment of life's facts, point of view, and how characters must fit the novel's demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of the novelist: reveal the hidden life
rubrics_metrics.description: “The novelist... to reveal the hidden ‘life « at its source: to tell us more about Queen Victoria than could be known, and thus to produce a character who is not the Queen Victoria of history.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist's central task is to expose inner life that history cannot: invent or reconstruct what lies behind observable actions. The novelist may plausibly supply inner motives, thoughts and private experience that are not available as historical evidence; this creative revelation distinguishes fiction from historical record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelistic method: thought developing into action (vs history's fatality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrase of Alain: “What is fictitious in a novel is not so much the story as the method by which thought develops into action.... History, with its emphasis on external causes, is dominated by the notion of fatality, whereas there is no fatality in the novel; there, everything is founded on human nature, and the dominating feeling is of an existence where everything is intentional.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or create fiction by whether inner thought logically (or artfully) leads to actions; characters act from intentions rather than being driven by fatal external causes. The novelist invents plausible internal causal chains that make actions intelligible in human, not solely external, terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters can be fully known to the reader if the novelist wishes
rubrics_metrics.description: “people in a novel can be understood completely by the reader, if the novelist wishes; their inner as well as their outer life can be exposed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novel may grant the reader total psychological access to characters — an aesthetic choice. When full knowledge is provided (or convincingly suggested), readers accept invented inner lives; when withheld, the novelist must still make the character feel explicable. This is a criterion for how much authorial knowledge/omniscience the work displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of the five main facts of life: birth, food, sleep, love, death
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay lists five main facts: birth, food, sleep, love and death, and asks whether novelists reproduce them accurately or exaggerate/minimize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how a novel handles these elemental experiences: birth and death are 'experiences and not experiences' (largely known by report) — novelists may start or end at convenient points; death is often handled richly because it 'ends a book neatly' and is 'nourished by observation'; food and sleep tend to be treated perfunctorily (food as social device; sleep/dreams condensed or schematic); love is frequently overemphasized and used as a convenient engine or ending (marriage/permanence). Craft decisions should reflect these tendencies deliberately rather than by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character realism: convincingness and adherence to a novel's laws of art
rubrics_metrics.description: “A novel is a work of art, with its own laws... a character in a novel is real when it lives in accordance with such laws. ... They are real not because they are like ourselves (though they may be like us) but because they are convincing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge or create characters by their internal consistency and plausibility within the novel's own aesthetic. 'Real' fictional people need not mirror everyday people exactly; they must convincingly obey the patterns and rules established by the work (tone, perspective, narrative logic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological completeness: the novelist must 'know everything' about a character
rubrics_metrics.description: “A character in a book is real: it is real when the novelist knows everything about it. ... He will give us the feeling that though the character has not been explained, it is explicable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For believable characters the author should have a sense of full biography/psychology (even if not disclosed). The important effect is that the reader senses the character is explicable and coherent; implied unseen detail gives credibility. Lack of this depth risks flatness or incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters' interdependence and world-embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in complex novels are 'bound by a hundred threads' to setting and to other characters (example: Miss Bates in Austen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many novels characters must be interwoven — their identities arise from relationships, social networks, and the plot. Assess whether characters are properly anchored in their world: can they be plausibly removed or transplanted? If not, that interdependence is a feature to be preserved; if characters are isolated (like Moll Flanders), that is an intentional, different mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between character freedom and authorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: “They 'run away,' they 'get out of hand': they are creations inside a creation, and often inharmonious towards it; if they are given complete freedom they kick the book to pieces, and if they are kept too sternly in check, they revenge themselves by dying, and destroy it by intestinal decay.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novelist must calibrate how much autonomy characters have: too much freedom can derail plot/structure; too little can make characters inert or cause contrived deaths. Evaluate whether characters' actions feel emergent and inevitable without undermining the planned architecture of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of different character kinds as a device (flat vs round)
rubrics_metrics.description: “We may divide characters into flat and round. Flat characters... are constructed round a single idea or quality... The really flat character can be expressed in one sentence... When there is more than one factor in them, we get the beginning of the curve towards the round.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately choose flat (type) or round (complex) characters according to narrative need. Flat characters are economical, immediately recognizable and durable; round characters develop, surprise, and are remembered through their changes. Assess whether each character's degree of complexity suits its narrative function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of flat characters: recognizability, ease, and endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are 'easily recognized whenever they come in' and 'easily remembered by the reader afterwards' — they remain unalterable because they 'were not changed by circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters serve economy of storytelling: they do not require reintroduction, do not 'run away', and provide a stable emotional shorthand. Use them when the novel needs immediately graspable figures or to create lasting impressions; beware of overuse which can flatten the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view and other instinctive devices for handling characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's devices to solve difficulties include 'the use of different kinds of characters' and 'the point of view.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose point of view deliberately as a tool to control what the reader knows about characters (how much inner life is revealed, who narrates, and what perspective shapes events). Point of view alters the perceivable inner/outer life and therefore determines the novel's psychological reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal visibility of secret life determines a character's plausibility in our world
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters like Moll Flanders cannot be 'here' because they 'belong to a world where the secret life is visible' — our everyday secret lives are invisible and thus differ from many fictional people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting characters, decide whether their 'secret life' is visible to the reader (and to other characters) or remains concealed. If a novel's world makes private motives transparent, its inhabitants will behave differently from ordinary people; maintain that internal logic consistently so readers accept the world-building choice.
